title: Myeolchi Bokkeum
subtitle: Sweet and sticky stir-fried dried anchovies
excerpt: Myeolchi bokkeum is a Korean banchan of small dried anchovies stir-fried quickly in a sweet soy and mirin glaze. It takes 15 minutes and serves 4 as a side dish. The anchovies caramelise until sticky and slightly crisp, making this one of the most addictive small dishes in the Korean repertoire.
sourceNotes: Myeolchi bokkeum has been a fixture of Korean home cooking for generations, appearing daily on tables across the country as one of the standard banchan. Dried anchovies have been a cornerstone of the Korean pantry for centuries, used both as a flavouring base for stocks and as a standalone ingredient in stir-fries and soups.

recipe.batchNotes: Keeps in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 5 days. The texture remains good at room temperature or cold.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Can be made up to 5 days in advance and stored in the fridge. Serve at room temperature.

glossaryTerms.definition: Banchan are the small side dishes served alongside rice at a Korean meal. They range from simple seasoned vegetables to fermented kimchi, braised tofu, and stir-fried anchovies. Several banchan are always present at once, and diners share them from the centre of the table. The number of banchan on a table traditionally reflected the wealth and generosity of the host.

Myeolchi is the Korean word for dried anchovies. They come in several sizes: large ones are used to make broth, while the small ones used in myeolchi bokkeum are about 3 to 5cm long. They have an intense, deeply savoury flavour that mellows into a sweet nuttiness when stir-fried with sugar and soy sauce.

content.text: bokkeum uses small dried anchovies stir-fried in a glaze of soy sauce, mirin, and sugar until sticky and slightly crisp. It is one of the most common side dishes on a Korean table and keeps well in the fridge for several days.

The key to this dish is dry-toasting the anchovies before adding any sauce. Toast them in the pan without oil for 2 to 3 minutes until they lose their fishy smell and become lightly golden. This step removes excess moisture and ensures they stay crisp rather than turning soggy in the glaze. Watch the heat when you add the sugar: it burns quickly.

items.prepNote: small dried anchovies, heads and innards intact
optional, for a hint of heat

content.text: Place the anchovies in a dry frying pan over medium heat. Toast, stirring occasionally, for 2 to 3 minutes until they are lightly golden and the fishy smell has mellowed. Remove from the pan and set aside.
Mix together the soy sauce, sugar, mirin, and gochugaru if using in a small bowl to make the sauce.
Add the oil to the same pan over medium heat. Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Return the anchovies to the pan and pour over the sauce. Toss continuously for 1 to 2 minutes until the sauce coats the anchovies and becomes sticky. Do not let the sugar burn.
Remove from the heat immediately. Drizzle with sesame oil and scatter over the sesame seeds. Serve at room temperature alongside rice and other banchan.

items.symptom: The anchovies are soft and soggy rather than slightly crisp
items.cause: The dry-toasting step was skipped or the sauce was added before the anchovies were properly dried out
items.fix: Always toast the anchovies first in a dry pan. If already sauced, spread them on a baking tray and dry in a low oven at 150C for 10 minutes

items.symptom: The glaze burns and becomes bitter
items.cause: The heat was too high when the sugar sauce was added
items.fix: Reduce to medium heat before adding the sauce and keep tossing constantly. The sauce needs only 1 to 2 minutes to coat the anchovies; it caramelises fast

items.cause: Dried anchovies are already salty and some brands are saltier than others
items.fix: Rinse the anchovies briefly in cold water before toasting, then pat completely dry. Reduce the soy sauce to half a tablespoon

content.text: Myeolchi bokkeum is one of the most common banchan in Korea. It appears in school lunchboxes, at home meals, and in restaurant spreads. Because it keeps for several days in the fridge, it is often made in advance and served over multiple meals. Dried anchovies are one of the most important ingredients in the Korean pantry: the large ones make the stock that forms the base of many soups, while the small ones become this sticky stir-fry. Once you have the anchovies and the sauce components to hand, this dish takes less time to make than it takes to describe.
